A gadabout is a person who is constantly going out and moving from place to place, always chasing fun, entertainment, excitement, or the company of others — rather than staying home or tending to their responsibilities.

The word is a noun, so it refers to a type of person.

Picture someone who is almost never at home. They are always at a party, a social gathering, a dinner, a trip, or some outing. The moment one event ends, they are already planning the next. They are restless. Sitting quietly at home feels unbearable to them. They constantly crave activity, excitement, and social stimulation.

That is a gadabout.

The key ingredients are:

  • Constant movement — they are always going somewhere.
  • Social motivation — the goal is pleasure, fun, or being around people.
  • Restlessness — they struggle to stay put.
  • A lack of seriousness — their wandering is not for work or a meaningful purpose; it is purely for a good time.

This is important: gadabout is not a compliment. It is not a harsh insult either, but it carries a mildly critical or disapproving tone. When someone calls another person a gadabout, they are subtly suggesting that this person is a little frivolous, irresponsible, or too focused on pleasure. There is an implication that the gadabout may be neglecting their duties, their family, or their home life in favor of constantly chasing social fun.

Think of it as a word used by someone who is slightly exasperated or judgmental — perhaps a strict parent talking about a neighbor, or a responsible older person describing a carefree young adult.

It is also a somewhat old-fashioned and informal word. You would not hear it in a formal speech or a scientific paper. You would hear it in casual conversation, in older novels, or in light-hearted writing.

• "She's such a gadabout — she's been to five parties this week and hasn't cooked a meal at home all month."
  • "My uncle was a gadabout in his youth, always travelling from city to city, chasing excitement wherever he could find it."
  • "Stop being a gadabout and stay home for once!"
  • "The neighbors called her a gadabout behind her back because she was always out socializing instead of looking after her garden."

Notice in each sentence — the gadabout is not doing anything truly terrible. They are just seen as someone who prioritizes fun and social life too much, at the expense of more grounded, responsible living.

To sharpen your understanding, here is what separates a gadabout from similar ideas:

  • A gadabout is not just a traveller. A traveller may explore the world for meaningful reasons — culture, learning, work. A gadabout roams specifically for socializing and amusement.
  • A gadabout is not just a sociable person. A sociable person enjoys company but can also stay home contentedly. A gadabout cannot seem to stay home — there is a restless, almost compulsive quality to their going out.
  • A gadabout is not a troublemaker. The word does not suggest bad behavior or wrongdoing. The criticism is simply about being too carefree and too pleasure-seeking.

Imagine a person in a small town who everyone knows — not because they do anything important, but because they are everywhere, all the time. At every social event, every gathering, every outing. People shake their heads affectionately (or with mild irritation) and say, "Oh, there goes the town gadabout." That image captures the word perfectly.

A gadabout is a person who is always out socializing and seeking amusement, restlessly moving from one place or event to another, and who is seen as a little too carefree about their responsibilities as a result.
